knowledge_type_note: A historical school, so its claims are teaching principles of their time rather than timeless truths. Mandatory hedging applies: several of its positions were corrections to a dogma rather than laws in their own right.

attributions.note: Originated the term 'hypermodern'; his Die hypermoderne Schachpartie appeared in 1924.
Considered the founder and leading practitioner; My System (1925-27) is the school's central text.
Die neuen Ideen im Schachspiel (1922) traced the evolution of chess thinking to the new school.

history.notes: Unusually well dated: three named books with years, an agreed founder, and an agreed coiner of the term. Recorded high because two independent sources agree on all of it, though none of the primary texts beyond My System was consulted.

development.change: My System published in five installments.
The openings are absorbed by everyone, including Capablanca and Tarrasch. The polemic dies down.
Treated as an extension of classical theory rather than a rival to it.

engine_era_note: Engines are comfortable with hypermodern structures and have vindicated several specific openings, but they do not support the polemical claim. A pawn centre that can be supported is simply good, and engines build one readily.

preconditions: An opening or plan that declines central occupation in favour of piece pressure
indicators_for: Fianchettoed bishops aimed at the centre
The opponent invited to build a pawn centre
An undermining break prepared against that centre
Restraint and prophylaxis as the plan
indicators_against: The centre is ceded with no undermining break available — that is not hypermodern play, it is passivity
The opponent's centre is properly supported and expanding on schedule
false_positive_traps: A fianchetto is not by itself hypermodern. The school's claim is about the centre, and a fianchetto with no plan against a central pawn mass is just a bishop on a long diagonal.
Ceding the centre without a break is not hypermodern; it is the failure mode the school itself warned about.
Attributing every modern positional idea to hypermodernism. Several were understood by Staunton's generation.

typical_plans: Invite the pawn centre, fix it, then undermine it with a break
Restrain first, blockade, then destroy — Nimzowitsch's formula
Fianchetto and pressure the centre from the flank
typical_pawn_structures: Opponent's broad pawn centre awaiting an undermining break
strategic_consequences: Introduced restraint and prophylaxis as plans in their own right

exceptions: The school's own central claim fails as a rule: cede the centre against proper support and you lose to space.
It did not replace classical theory and was absorbed into it within a decade.
Several of its ideas predate it in nineteenth-century practice.
limitations: A historical school rather than a technique; its content is now distributed across other concepts (outpost, blockade, prophylaxis, overprotection, restraint).
misconceptions: That hypermodernism beat classical theory. Textbooks present it as an extension of it.
That hypermoderns thought the centre unimportant.

examples.note: Reti-Capablanca, New York 1924, after 8.d3 - the game the school is usually taught from, and the annotation is the school's own founder describing the system he is playing: Reti in Masters of the Chessboard, 'The move directs pressure against the centre, prevents 1...e5, and keeps open almost all the possibilities for the first player.' White has not one pawn on a central square. His influence over d4, e4 and e5 comes from a bishop on the long diagonal, a knight on f3 and pawns on c4 and d3, which is the ground principle of the record stated as a position. Capablanca is about to occupy the centre with ...e5 and lose. Corpus entry `reti-capablanca-1924-8d3-center-control-ambiguous` reads the same position for `center-control`, where it is ambiguous; here it is not, because what is being illustrated is the METHOD rather than who stands better.
examples.attributed_by: Richard Reti, Masters of the Chessboard - corpus entry reti-capablanca-1924-8d3-center-control-ambiguous

engine.verdict_note: -0.27 from Black's side: the player with NO pawn on a central square is the one very slightly better. That is a small number and it is the right size - the hypermodern claim is that the indirect method is sound, not that it wins, and an example evaluating at +1.5 would be evidence for a different and false proposition.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-fianchetto-with-nothing-behind-it`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Both sides have fianchettoed. Bishops on g2 and g7 on the long diagonals, knights on f3 and f6, no pawn on e4 or e5 — the hypermodern picture, twice. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The ground principle is to control the centre INDIRECTLY with pieces, inviting the opponent to occupy it so the pawns become targets. Neither bishop bears on anything: g2 is blocked by its own knight on f3 and by the d4 pawn beyond it, g7 by its own knight on f6 and the d5 pawn. Nobody is being invited to occupy anything, and the centre is already symmetrically fixed. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports nothing here at all. +0.27 at depth 22, settled at depth 21 — an ordinary symmetrical position. The case is registered because the fianchetto is the most recognisable thing about the school and is the part that carries none of the content: this record's positive example, Reti-Capablanca after 8.d3, has White's bishop on b2 bearing down an OPEN long diagonal at a centre Black is about to occupy. The picture is nearly the same and the idea is absent.

ambiguous_examples.note: Reti-Capablanca 1924, move 18 - the canonical hypermodern game, in which the annotator's advice to the losing side is classical. Keene: 'it is a mystery why Capablanca did not play the obvious 18...Ne6, fighting more directly for control of the centre.' Fighting for the centre is the thing hypermodernism was a reaction against being dogmatic about, and here it is the recommendation, inside the game the school is taught from, given against the player the school beat. Filed as ambiguous because both readings survive: Reti's system won by controlling the centre from a distance, and Capablanca's error was not contesting it directly enough, and those are the same claim about central control read from two schools.
ambiguous_examples.attributed_by: Raymond Keene (GM), The Spectator Australia - corpus entry reti-capablanca-1924-18Ne6-center-control

engine.verdict_note: +0.80, and the engine's first choice is the move Keene recommends. Both candidate knight moves develop and neither occupies a central square; what separates them is how much they contest d4 and c5, which is the hypermodern criterion applied to a classical recommendation.

by_level.beginner: A group of players in the 1920s argued you do not have to put pawns in the middle — you can aim pieces at it from far away and let your opponent's pawns become targets.
by_level.intermediate: Hypermodernism: control the centre with pieces, invite the pawn centre, then undermine it. It is a correction to the older rule, not a replacement for it.
by_level.advanced: The 1920s reaction to Tarrasch's dogma. Its lasting contributions are restraint, prophylaxis, the blockade and the outpost, more than the central polemic itself.
by_level.master: Read it as a set of exceptions rather than a system — Réti said as much. Ceding the centre without a concrete break is the failure mode the school itself identified.

by_depth.short: Control the centre with pieces instead of occupying it with pawns.
by_depth.normal: The hypermodern school, from the 1920s: control the centre from a distance rather than occupying it, and let the opponent's pawn centre become a target. It produced the Nimzo-Indian, Grünfeld, King's Indian and Réti, along with restraint, prophylaxis and the blockade.
by_depth.deep: A post-war movement led by Nimzowitsch and Réti, with Tartakower coining the name in 1924. Its target was Tarrasch's dogmatic codification of Steinitz rather than Steinitz himself, and Réti characterised the generation as interested not in rules but in exceptions. Its concrete legacy outlived the polemic — the fianchetto revived as a central weapon, restraint and prophylaxis as plans, the blockade, overprotection, the outpost. What it did not do is win: by the late 1920s its openings had been absorbed by everyone including Capablanca and Tarrasch, and modern textbooks treat it as an addition to classical theory rather than a replacement. Its own limit is honest and well known — cede the centre as a principle against an opponent who supports theirs and expands on time, and you lose to the space you invited.

explanations.hedge: A historical school, not a set of laws. Its central claim was a corrective to a prevailing dogma and fails when applied as a dogma itself: ceding the centre without a concrete plan to undermine it simply concedes space.
explanations.lesson: The hypermodern insight worth keeping is that controlling a square and standing on it are different things. The polemic around it is history.

beginner_words: control the middle from far away

definition_short: The 1920s movement holding that the centre should be controlled from a distance with pieces rather than occupied with pawns, and that a committed pawn centre is a target.
definition_long:
A school that emerged after the First World War, led by Nimzowitsch and Réti with Tartakower supplying the slogans, and including Breyer, Bogoljubov and Grünfeld — all Central European. Its target was not Steinitz but Tarrasch's dogmatic codification of him.

The ground principle: control the centre indirectly with pieces, inviting the opponent to occupy it with pawns so those pawns become targets. Réti's summary of the generation was that they were interested 'not in rules but in exceptions', and Breyer's joke — 'after the first move 1.e4 White's game is in the last throes' — was the provocation in concentrated form.

It produced a body of concrete ideas that outlived the polemic: the fianchetto revived as a central weapon, restraint and prophylaxis as plans in their own right, the blockade, overprotection, the outpost, the pawn chain, and the openings that carry the names — Nimzo-Indian, Queen's Indian, Grünfeld, Réti, King's Indian, Alekhine's Defence.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED TO IT is the part usually got wrong. It did not win and did not replace classical theory. Modern textbooks describe it as an ADDITION to classical theory, and by the late 1920s its openings had been absorbed by everyone, Capablanca and Tarrasch included. Its own honest limit is that ceding the centre as a principle, against an opponent who supports the resulting mass and expands on time, loses to the space advantage invited — so it is a correction to a dogma rather than a replacement dogma.

Historically it was also less novel than it presented itself: Staunton and other nineteenth-century players understood several of the ideas, and the fianchetto had simply fallen out of fashion after Morphy popularised open centres.
